Enhancing anaerobic digestion of swine manure using microbial 
electrolysis cell and microaeration
Yanqiang Di a,1, Wenxue Hou b,1, Chunlin Bian b,c, Tianlong Zheng b, Benyi Xiao b,*
, Lin Li b
a China Academy of Building Research, Beijing 100013, China
b Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100085, China
c Jiangsu Jiangnan Water Co., Ltd., Jiangyin 214400, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Microaeration
Microbial electrolysis cell
Swine manure
Synergistic effect
A B S T R A C T
To enhance anaerobic digestion (AD) of swine manure (SW) and decrease the hydrogen sulfide (H2S) concen­
tration in biogas, microbial electrolysis cell (MEC) and microaeration (MA) were applied, and semi-continuous 
experiments were conducted to compare their enhancements. The results showed that both MEC and MA 
enhanced the production of methane (24.74–68.24 %) and the removal of organic matter (8.54–23.80 %), 
increased the reaction rates of the four main AD steps (hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methano­
genesis), and boosted the activities of key enzymes, with MEC showing the greater increase. A slight synergistic 
effect was observed between MEC and MA. MA and MA combined with MEC (MM) decreased the H2S concen­
tration in biogas (67.93 ± 14.20 % and 12.94 ± 17.81 %) by enriching sulfur oxidizing bacteria, boosting sulfite 
oxidase activity, and restricting sulfite reductase activity. However, MEC increased the H2S concentration in 
biogas (175.26 ± 96.80 %) by enriching sulfate reducing bacteria and boosting the sulfite reductase activity. The 
three methods (MEC, MA, and MM) all enriched the hydrolytic and acidogenic bacteria and altered the pre­
dominant methanogenesis pathway. MEC and MM strengthened direct interspecies electron transfer by enriching 
Methanosaeta, Clostridium_sensu_stricto_1, and Romboutsia. Results from this study may offer some promising al­
ternatives for the energy issues faced by villages and small towns in China.
1. Introduction
China is the largest swine producer and swine meat consumer in the 
world. The huge demand for meat and rapid expansion of the swine 
farming industry have led to the large-scale generation of swine manure 
(SM) in China [1], which has reached approximately 0.6 billion tons 
annually [2,3]. Owing to its high chemical oxygen demand (COD) and 
nitrogen and phosphorus content, SM causes serious environmental 
problems (such as eutrophication, odor, and pathogen transmission) and 
has become an important agricultural source of pollution in villages and 
small towns in China [2,3]. For example, SM can cause eutrophication of 
fresh water resources due to its high content of nitrogen (N) and phos­
phates (P), while the emission of odors and volatile compounds from SM 
can significantly impact human health due to the high ammonia and 
volatile compounds content [4]. However, SM is also regarded as a 
resource, with farmers applying it as a fertilizer to enhance crop pro­
duction for centuries [4]. Therefore, the treatment of SM has become a 
challenge for maximum productivity with minimum environmental 
impact and appropriate treatment of SM is important.
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is considered a promising and environ­
mentally sustainable technology for SM treatment because it can convert 
organic matter into bioenergy (methane and hydrogen), reduce the 
amount of SM, and generate organic fertilizers [5,6]. In addition, the AD 
of SM can provide bioenergy for villages and small towns in China, 
where swine farming is predominantly located. However, the AD of SM 
has certain shortcomings, such as slow hydrolysis-acidification rate, low 
methane yield, insufficient substrate utilization, and high amounts of 
solid and liquid digestates [5,6]. Previous studies have shown that the 
methane yield of SM ranged from 220 to 438 mL/g volatile solids (VS), 
which is far lower than its theoretical value (720 mL/g VS) [7,8]. 
Moreover, there is also a problem of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) production 
during the AD of SM, which inhibits methanogens and corrodes equip­
ment and pipelines [9,10]. A previous study [11] showed that the sulfur 
content of SM is 5.56–5.99 g/kg total solids (TS). Therefore, to produce

more high-quality bioenergy for villages and small towns in China, the 
AD of SM must be enhanced. Many methods and strategies have been 
developed to enhance this process, including pretreatment, co-digestion 
with high C/N organic matter, thermophilic digestion, adding additives, 
microbial electrolysis cell (MEC), and microaeration (MA) [12–14].
MEC is driven by electrogenic microorganisms under a low applied 
external voltage and considered a promising method for enhancing AD 
[15,16]. This environmentally friendly bio-electrochemical technology 
was first applied to produce biohydrogen from various organic wastes 
[6,15]. Recently, MEC has been used to enhance the AD of organic 
wastes by promoting electron transfer, enriching functional microor­
ganisms, and changing the methanogenesis pathways [15,17]. MEC can 
increase electron transfer by strengthening the direct interspecies elec­
tron transfer (DIET) pathway, which is considered a promising strategy 
to improve the performance of AD [16]. Previous studies [14,18,19] 
have reported that MEC can improve the AD of SM. For example, Zou 
et al. [14] found that MEC with an applied voltage of 0.9 V increased the 
maximum cumulative biogas yields from 401.7 mL/g TS to 547.3 mL/g 
TS and the methane yield from 347.7 mL/g TS to 224.0 mL/g TS in batch 
AD of SM.
MA, namely, dosing a small amount of oxygen or air to the AD sys­
tem, is another promising method for enhancing AD [20,21]. MA has 
recently been considered an attractive and effective strategy to enhance 
AD. MA-based AD has been defined as a micro-aerobic condition with an 
oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) ranging from −300 to 0 mV, as 
determined by a standard hydrogen electrode [21]. Micro-oxygen 
dosing enriches the facultative acidogens and increases the bacterial 
diversity during AD [21]. Moreover, it can promote the oxidation of 
sulfide, which decreases the concentration of H2S in biogas [22]. 
Therefore, MA can enhance AD by accelerating hydrolysis and acidifi­
cation, scavenging H2S and reducing its concentration in biogas, 
improving process stabilization, regulating microbial communities, and 
promoting methane production through the supply of a small amount of 
oxygen [21–23]. Previous studies have found that MA can enhance the 
hydrolysis and acidification of SM [24] and promote organic matter 
removal and methane production rate in swine wastewater treatment 
[12].
Although MEC and MA present different mechanisms for enhancing 
AD, previous studies have not compared their enhancement effects. 
Moreover, considering the special characteristics of SM (such as high 
organic content and containing sulfur compounds), it is expected that 
MEC and MA can synergistically enhance the AD of SM by exerting their 
respective advantages when they are co-integrated. However, no study 
has yet addressed this topic. Therefore, to fill this gap, this study inno­
vatively integrates MEC and MA and compares their individual and 
synergistic effects on the AD of SM. The performances (biogas produc­
tion and quality, matter conversion, and digestate characteristics), re­
action rates of the four AD steps, functional enzyme activities, and 
microbial community structures of the AD processes were evaluated. 
The objective is to explore the synergistic enhancements and mecha­
nisms of MEC and MA and identify an effective method of boosting the 
AD of SM to help resolve the energy issues in villages and small towns in 
China.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Swine manure and inoculum
The SM used in this study was obtained from a pig farm in Beijing, 
China. After collection, the SM was ground in a blender (QH-400D, 
Qihui, China) and then manually screened through a 40 mesh sieve to 
remove large particles. The pretreated SM was stored at 4 ◦C until use. 
The digestate used as the inoculum in the experiments was obtained 
from a lab-scale mesophilic anaerobic digester, which used SM as a 
substrate. The main characteristics of the SM and inoculum are sum­
marized in Table 1.
2.2. Anaerobic digesters
Four identical lab-scale continuous stirred tank reactors (CSTRs) 
with total and working volumes of 5 L and 3.9 L, respectively, were used 
as anaerobic digesters. Two electrodes were integrated into each 
digester with a distance of 2 cm. The electrodes were composed of a 
carbon rod (diameter × height = 8 × 350 mm) and ten square carbon 
felts (length × width × thickness = 60 × 30 × 5 mm), which is similar to 
those used in previous study [17] (Fig. S1).
2.3. Operation of the anaerobic digesters
The four ADs were first inoculated with 3.9 L of inoculum and purged 
with high-purity nitrogen (99.99 %) for 5 min to eliminate oxygen and 
create anaerobic conditions. One digester (MA-AD) was continuously 
aerated with a micro-aerator (BT100-2 J, Longer Co., China) at an 
aeration rate of 0.014 L/L/d (based on the working volume) [25,26]. 
The second digester (MEC-AD) was operated at 1.2 V applied voltage 
through a DC power supply [17,27]. The third digester (MM-AD) was 
simultaneously subjected to 1.2 V voltage and continuously aerated at a 
rate of 0.014 L/L/d. The last digester (Con-AD), which was not con­
nected to the DC power supply applied voltage and not aerated, served 
as the control. The four ADs were maintained at 37 ± 1◦C using heaters 
(CH-1006, Hengping Co., China) and water jackets, and mixed at a 
stirring rate of 300 rpm. Subsequently, the digesters were started up in a 
semi-continuous mode with daily discharge and feeding using gastight 
glass syringes. The hydraulic retention times (HRTs) of the four ADs 
were decreased from 100 d to 30 d over 2 weeks by gradually increasing 
the feed, and then the digesters were operated for 88 d at an HRT of 30 d. 
The four ADs were operated for 104 d in total, with the operation period 
dividing into start-up (0–30 d), adjustment (31–60 d), and stable 
(61–104 d) stages.
2.4. Analytical methods
The biogas produced from the four ADs was stored in gas bags, and 
its volume was measured every two days by replacing saturated NaCl 
aqueous solution [6]. The methane (CH4) content and H2S concentration 
in the biogas were measured using two gas chromatographs (GCs): one 
equipped with a flame ionization detector (Agilent 6890 N, USA) for 
CH4, and the other with a flame photometric detector (Agilent 6890, 
USA) for H2S [17].
The influents (substrate, SM) and effluents (anaerobic digestates) of 
the four ADs were sampled and analyzed twice a week. The analytical 
parameters included total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), chemical ox­
ygen demand (COD), pH, ORP, total ammonia nitrogen (TAN), total 
alkalinity (TA), and volatile fatty acids (VFAs). The analytical methods 
were the same as those used in previous studies [6,17] and the ORP was 
measured using a multi-parameter portable meter (WTW Multi 3630 
IDS, Langenhagen, Germany). The total sulfur content was measured 
using an elemental analyzer (CHWKL-0253, Shanghai Changai, China). 
Sulfate (SO4
2-) was measured using ion chromatography (ICS3000, Dio­
nex, Sunnyvale, CA, USA); sulfide (S2-) was measured using a gas-phase 
molecular absorption spectrometer (GMA3376, Shanghai Beiyu, China);

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Biogas production
Biogas production of the four ADs was measured, and the results 
were summarized in Fig. 1 and Table 2. The results showed that biogas 
production of all four ADs gradually increased during the start-up stage 
(0–30 d), fluctuated during the adjustment stage (31–60 d), and then 
entered the stable stage, with averages of 0.58 ± 0.03 L/L/d (Con-AD), 
0.75 ± 0.04 L/L/d (MA-AD), 0.92 ± 0.03 L/L/d (MEC-AD), and 0.96 ±
0.02 L/L/d (MM-AD) (Fig. 1-a and Table 2). The methane contents in the 
biogas produced from the four ADs were relatively stable during the 
adjustment and stable stages and ranged from 52.57 % to 79.67 %. The 
methane contents of MEC-AD and MM-AD (63.17 ± 0.98 % and 61.86 
± 1.27 %, respectively) were higher than those of Con-AD (61.11 ±
2.11 %) and MA-AD, which had the lowest content (59.20 ± 1.42 %) 
(Fig. 1-b and Table 2). Statistical analysis showed that the methane 
contents in the biogas produced from Con-AD and MM-AD were similar 
(p = 0.12 > 0.05, Table S1) and significantly different from those of the 
other two ADs (p < 0.05, Table S1).
Methane production of the four ADs was obtained from biogas pro­
duction and methane content (Fig. 1-c). The changes in methane pro­
duction were similar to those in biogas production, and the methane 
production of Con-AD was the lowest (Fig. 1-c and Table 2). The results 
indicated that MEC and MA enhanced the production of biogas and 
methane at rates of 28.21–65.97 % and 24.74–68.24 %, respectively 
(Table S2) [15,21], and MEC presented a greater enhancing effect than 
MA. Synergism was also observed when MEC and MA were co-integrated 
during the AD of SM (Table S2). The coefficients of variation (Table S3) 
showed that the three methods (MEC, MA, and MM) decreased the 
variations in methane content and methane production. Therefore, MEC 
and MA enhanced the stability of methane production [15,21]. In 
addition, the three methods presented greater enhancing effects on the 
AD of SM relative to those reported in most previous studies (Table 3). 
For example, Liu et al. [5] found that MEC enhanced the methane yield 
of SM by 60.89 % and de Oliveira et al. [12] found that MA enhanced the 
methane yield of swine wastewater by 57.54 %.

also measured (Fig. 1-d). The results showed that the H2S concentrations

3.2. Changes in the liquid phase
The digestate characteristics were detected during the experiment, 
and their changes are shown in Fig. 2. During the stable stage, the ORPs 
of MA-AD and MM-AD (−228 to −
286 mV and −
289 to −
300 mV, 
respectively) were higher than that of Con-AD and MEC-AD (−316 to −
328 mV and −
331 to −
340 mV, respectively) (Fig. 2-A and Table S4). 
These results indicated that the former two digesters were under micro- 
aerobic conditions and the latter two were under anaerobic conditions 
[21]. The pH of the digestates from the four ADs ranged from 7.68 to 
8.15, which was similar to previous studies [17,32]. The TAN concen­
trations in the digestates from the four ADs gradually increased during 
the start-up and adjustment stages and reached a relatively steady level 
during the stable stage (Fig. 2-c). During the stable stage, the TAN 
concentration in digestate from Con-AD was the lowest (with an average 
of 3.66 ± 0.32 g/L), while that from MM-AD was the highest (with an 
average of 4.19 ± 0.28 g/L) (Fig. 2-c and Table S4). The results indicated 
that MA and MEC promoted the anaerobic conversion of nitrogen- 
containing substances (mainly proteins) and presented synergistic ef­
fects since TAN is a product of the anaerobic conversion of nitrogen- 
containing substances [44]. TAN toxicity is a known problem for AD 
and the reported TAN inhibitory threshold ranged between 1.50–7.00 g/ 
L [45]. Therefore, TAN inhibition may occur in the four ADs. Free 
ammonia (FAN) is the active component that causes ammonia inhibition 
which depends mainly on TAN, temperature, and pH. During the stable 
stage, the FAN concentration in digestate from MEC-AD was the lowest 
(0.90 ± 0.00 g/L), while that from MM-AD was the highest (1.06 ± 0.00 
g/L) (Table S4) [32]. The results indicated that the inhibition of TAN in 
the MM-AD was the highest and that in MEC-AD was the lowest. In other 
words, the three methods affected the TAN inhibition in the AD of SM.
The total VFAs (TVFAs) concentration in digestates from the four 
ADs ranged from 0.03 to 0.43 mg/L, which were far lower than that of 
the SM (7.04 mg/L to 9.73 mg/L), indicating that VFA accumulation did 
not occur during the experiment [46,47]. The low TVFAs concentrations 
in digestates also suggested that the TAN inhibition on methanogens was 
low. The digestates from the four ADs had high TA concentrations 
(9.01–15.51 g CaCO3/L), indicating that the digestates had a good buffer 
ability [46]. The TVFA/TA ratios for the four ADs during the experiment 
were all lower than 0.3 (Fig. 2-f), indicating that the four ADs had stable 
operations [17]. The TS, VS, and total chemical oxygen demand (TCOD) 
concentrations in digestates from the four ADs during the experiment 
were also relatively stable, with Con-AD and MM-AD presenting the 
highest and lowest average values, respectively (Fig. 2-g-i and Table S4). 
Additionally, statistical analysis indicated that the TS, VS, and TCOD 
concentrations in digestates from the four ADs were significantly 
different (p < 0.05; Table S1). The results suggested that the three 
methods enhanced the removal of organic matter at an enhancement 
rate of 8.54–23.80 % (Fig. S2), which was consistent with the production 
of methane [46].

3.3. Mass balance based on COD and sulfur
The mass balances based on COD for the four ADs during the stable 
stage are summarized in Fig. 3-a. Particle COD (PCOD) is an important 
component of SM and the digestates from the four ADs and accounted 
for 39.40–78.90 % of the COD, which was far higher than that of soluble 
COD (SCOD) (4.09–21.10 %). The content of CH4-COD in MM-AD 
(59.13 ± 3.16 %) was the highest, followed by that in MEC-AD (57.82 
± 2.51 %) and Con-AD (35.26 ± 1.25 %), which was consistent with 
their CH4 production (Fig. 1 and Table 2). The COD-gap value was also 
the highest (11.87 ± 0.41 %) in Con-AD and the lowest (−2.62 ± 0.09 
%) in MM-AD. The results indicated that all three methods decreased the 
COD-gap. In other words, both MEC and MA decreased the loss of COD 
and the invalid anaerobic conversion of organic matter, exhibiting a 
slight synergistic effect [17].
Among the four ADs, the total sulfur concentration in digestates from 
MA-AD (10.45 ± 0.56 mg/g TS) was the highest, while that from MEC- 
AD (8.25 ± 0.19 mg/g TS) was the lowest (Table S4), which was

MA-AD and MM-AD were higher than that in Con-AD, with that in MA-

enhanced the activity of sulfite reductase and did not affect the activity 
of sulfite oxidase, whereas MA and MM decreased the activity of sulfite 
reductase and increased the activity of sulfite oxidase [22]. The different 
activities of sulfite reductase and oxidase in the four ADs were consistent 
with the changes in sulfur (Fig. 3-b).
Previous studies [15,21] showed that both MA and MEC could 
accelerate the hydrolysis and acidogenesis of organic matter. Therefore, 
the reaction rates of hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and meth­
anogenesis (four main AD steps) were calculated (Fig. 4-b). Among the 
four ADs, the reaction rates of the four steps for Con-AD were the lowest 
while those for MM-AD were the highest, which were consistent with 
their methane production and enzyme activities (Fig. 1 and Fig. 4-a). 
This finding indicated that the three methods (MA, MEC, and MM) could 
accelerate the four AD steps and increase their reaction rates [15,21,32]. 
The reaction rates of MEC-AD (1.12–1.66 g COD/L/d) were higher than 
those of MA-AD (1.09–1.26 g COD/L/d), indicating that the enhancing 
effects of MEC were higher than those of MA. Meanwhile, MM-AD had 
the highest reaction rates (1.14–1.70 g COD/L/d) for the four AD steps, 
indicating that MA and MEC had a synergistic effect. The methano­
genesis rates of Con-AD and MA-AD were lower than their acidogenesis 
and acetogenesis rates, whereas the results of MEC-AD and MM-AD were 
opposite. This finding suggested that MA mainly affects the first three 
AD steps (hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and acetogenesis) [21] while MEC 
affects all four AD steps [15]. Additionally, although hydrolysis was 
enhanced by all three methods, the increase was the lowest among the 
four AD steps, indicating that it is still the rate-limiting step of AD [44].
3.5. Microbial community analysis
At the end of the stable period (102 d), the digestates from the four 
ADs were sampled to analyze the microbial communities. The alpha 
diversity estimators of the digestates from the four ADs are summarized 
in Table 4. The Chao and Shannon indices were higher for bacteria than 
archaea, indicating that the abundance and diversity of bacteria were 
higher than those of archaea [49]. The Chao and Shannon indices of 
bacteria were lowest for Con-AD among the four ADs, while those of 
archaea were the highest for Con-AD. These results suggested that these 
three methods increased the richness and diversity of bacteria and 
decreased the richness and diversity of archaea. MA can create a suitable 
environment for facultative bacteria and thereby increase the bacterial 
richness and diversity and inhibit strict anaerobic methanogens because 
micro-oxygen is harmful to such organisms [50]. In addition, MEC can 
enrich both functional bacteria and hydrogenotrophic methanogens 
[15].
3.5.1. Bacterial community
At the phylum level, Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, 
Actinobacteriota, and Chloroflexi represent the main hydrolytic and 
acidogenic bacteria in AD [51]. In this study, their total abundances 
ranged from 79.05 % to 93.54 % in the four ADs, with the highest 
observed in MA-AD and the lowest observed in Con-AD (Fig. 5-a). The 
results indicated that MEC and MA enriched the relative abundances of 
hydrolytic and acidogenic bacteria [51], with MA exhibiting greater 
enrichment than MEC. Meanwhile, synergistic effects were observed 
between MEC and MA. The enrichment of hydrolytic bacteria was 
consistent with the changes in the hydrolysis rate (Fig. 4-b).
At the genus level, Clostridium_sensu_stricto_1 was the dominant bac­
terial genus in the four ADs and had a relative abundance of 
29.02–33.19 % (Fig. 5-b). Romboutsia was the second bacterial genus 
(relative abundance of 7.71–10.33 %) in MEC-AD, MA-AD, and MM-AD, 
while unclassified_o_Cloacimonadales ranked second in Con-AD (relative 
abundance of 11.17 %). Both Clostridium_sensu_stricto_1 and Romboutsia 
belong to the phylum Firmicutes, which can convert organic matter 
(such as proteins and carbohydrates) into VFAs and hydrogen [52,53]. 
Previous studies also have found that Clostridium_sensu_stricto_1 was the

The results suggested that the predominant methanogenesis pathways in 
four ADs during the stable stage differed, with hydrogenotrophic 
pathway observed in Con-AD and acetoclastic and hydrogenotrophic 
pathways observed in the other three ADs (Table S6) [55,61,62]. It is 
reported that Methanosarcina has a higher growth rate and is more 
tolerant against different stressors and sudden environmental changes 
than the other methanogens. Methanosarcina can use both the aceto­
clastic and the hydrogenotrophic pathways [63]. Therefore, versatile 
methanogenesis can improve the biogas and CH4 production and the 
changes in the predominant methanogenesis pathway may explain the 
increase in methane production by MEC-AD, MA-AD, and MM-AD 
(Fig. 1-c) [15,62].
RDA (Fig. 6-b) indicated that hydrogenotrophic methanogens were 
significantly correlated with the organic characteristics of the digestates 
(TCOD, SCOD, VS, TS, VS/TS), versatile methanogens (Methanosarcina) 
were significantly correlated with the acidic characteristics of the 
digestates (pH, VFA, and acetic acid), and acetoclastic methanogens 
(Methanosaeta) were significantly correlated with the ammonic charac­
teristics of the digestates (TA and TAN) [60]. Methanosaeta and Candi­
datus_Methanofastidiosum were also positively correlated with gas 
production (biogas and methane production and methane content).
Previous studies have shown that Methanobacterium and Meth­
anosaeta are electroactive archaea that can perform the DIET and use 
carbon dioxide to produce methane by obtaining electrons from bacteria 
such as Clostridium_sensu_stricto_1 and Romboutsia [64,65]. The higher 
methane content in biogas produced from MEC-AD and MM-AD (Fig. 1- 
c) indicated that DIET occurred in the two ADs [65–67]. Additionally, 
the high concentration of acetic acid in the substrate (SM) (Table S4) 
resulted in the high relative abundance of Methanosaeta [68]. Although 
most methanogens are strict anaerobes and oxygen is lethal to them, 
some methanogens (e.g., Methanosarcina and Methanocella) can survive 
under microaerobic conditions [23]. This may explain why Meth­
anosarcina was enriched and dominant in MA-AD [21].
3.6. Implications
In this study, MEC, MA, and their integration (MM) were applied to 
AD of SM. The results demonstrated that both MEC and MA can enhance 
the AD of SM and revealed a synergistic effect between them. During the 
stable stage, the methane yield of SM in MM-AD was the highest (279.94 
± 17.59 mL/g VS), which was 67.70 ± 6.13 % higher than that in Con- 
AD (Table 2 and Table S2). Meanwhile, the H2S concentration in the 
biogas produced in MM-AD (1112 ± 219 ppmV) was 12.94 ± 17.81 % 
lower than that in Con-AD (1321 ± 342 ppmV). These results indicated 
that MEC operated in combination with MA can simultaneously increase 
the energy production of the AD of SM and improve its quality.
A key finding of this study is that MM can significantly increase 
biogas and methane production and upgrade biogas quality, indicating 
that more energy can be recovered from SM. This enhancement method 
is promising and easy to apply in practice because the energy inputs 
required for MEC and MA are very low [15,20,21]. Although the in­
crease in methane yield was only 113.02 ± 11.58 mL/g VS (from 166.93

4. Conclusion
Both MEC and MA enhanced methane production and organic matter 
removal in the AD of SM, with MEC showing a greater enhancement 
effect and MEC and MA showing a slight synergistic effect. MEC 
increased the H2S concentration in the biogas by enhancing the activity 
of sulfite reductase, whereas MA and MM decreased it by enhancing the 
activity of sulfite oxidase. These three methods enriched the hydrolytic 
and acidogenic bacteria and shifted the predominant methanogenesis 
pathway. However, further researches on the scalability of the findings 
and long-term performance and sustainability of scaled-up systems are 
required to meet the energy demands of villages and small towns in 
China.
